intro: Your body and your mind are a team. When you sleep well, you think more clearly. When you feel worried, your stomach may feel tight. When you run and play, your mood often lifts. In this unit, you will learn how the mind and body work together.

First, you will learn that mental health is part of health. You will learn what stress is and what helps, like breathing, moving, talking and sleep. You will meet the people who help, and learn that every mind works in its own way.

Then you will learn how bodies grow and change. You will learn about growth spurts, teeth, eyes, ears and muscles. By the end, you will be able to explain how to care for your whole self, and whom to ask when you have questions.
bigQuestion: How do our minds and bodies work together, and how can we care for both as we grow?

Doctor Philippe Pinel in Paris calls for kinder care of people with mental illness
Dorothea Dix travels the U.S. asking for better hospitals for people with mental illness
Wilhelm Wundt opens one of the first psychology labs, in Leipzig, Germany
The World Health Organization says health includes body, mind and life with others
A U.S. law gives children with disabilities the right to a free public education
The word neurodiversity comes into use to describe natural brain differences
The American Academy of Sleep Medicine publishes sleep advice for children
U.S. guidelines say kids ages 6 to 17 need at least 60 minutes of activity a day
The U.S. starts 988, a phone number to call or text for mental health help

test.q: Which part of the body is the control center that makes feelings?
test.why: The brain makes emotions and controls thinking and moving.

test.q: According to the World Health Organization, health includes which parts?
choices: Body, mind and life with others
test.why: The WHO describes physical, mental and social well-being.

test.q: Which tool can calm stress anywhere, even at your desk?
test.why: Slow belly breathing can be done anywhere and helps the body calm down.

test.q: About how much sleep do kids ages 6 to 12 need?
test.why: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine says 9 to 12 hours for ages 6 to 12.

test.q: Worry that is strong and lasts a long time may be called what?
test.why: Anxiety is strong worry that lasts a long time and gets in the way of daily life.

test.q: Who is a trained helper at school for feelings and friendships?
test.why: A school counselor supports students with feelings, friends and school problems.

test.q: What is an example of a support for a student who notices sounds strongly?
test.why: Headphones can help someone who notices sounds strongly.

test.q: Why is turning off screens before bed helpful?
choices: Bright screen light can delay melatonin
test.why: Bright light at night can trick the brain and delay the sleep hormone melatonin.

choices: Inviting them in and making room
test.why: Including means inviting someone in, listening and making room.

test.q: Why do growing kids often need more food and sleep?
choices: Their bodies are building new bone and muscle
test.why: Growing takes energy, and growth hormone is released during deep sleep.

test.q: Why can two kids of the same age be very different heights?
choices: One is eating the wrong color food
One of them is not healthy
Bodies grow at different times and genes differ
test.why: Genes and each body's own clock shape when and how much a child grows.

test.q: How many baby teeth do children have?
test.why: Children have 20 baby teeth that are later replaced by adult teeth.

test.q: What do the lenses in glasses do?
choices: Bend light so it focuses in the right spot
test.why: Lenses bend light so it focuses in the right spot in the eye.

test.q: Which helps protect your hearing at loud events?
test.why: Earplugs and lower volume help protect the ear's hair cells, which do not grow back.

test.q: Whom does this unit say to ask about body changes as you grow?
choices: A parent, school nurse or doctor
test.why: Parents, school nurses and doctors can give true answers about growing up.

write.prompt: Which matters more for a fourth grader's health: sleep or exercise? Make a claim. Use two or three facts from this unit to support it, and explain how your choice helps both the mind and the body.
tips: Start with one clear sentence that states your claim.
Name where each fact comes from, like the CDC or the American Academy of Sleep Medicine.
Explain how your choice helps both mind and body.
Say one good thing about the other choice, to be fair.
Use unit words like stress, melatonin or growth hormone.
